extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in undergraduate mathematics education; college mathematics instructors interested in use of examples
extracted.subtask_description: Method and criteria for documenting and analyzing the 'enacted example space' used in an undergraduate proof-based course (here: introductory abstract algebra), including how examples/non-examples are recorded, characterized, sequenced, used, and how student engagement is inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example log — item identity (column 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first column listed each example or non-example of the particular construct; in this case the construct was an algebraic group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record each distinct example/non-example explicitly (e.g., '(Z,+)', '(Q,+)', 'rationals under multiplication'). Use problem-stems that indicate students were to consider a particular example (e.g., 'determine if the following form a group', 'Show that X is a group').

rubrics_metrics.name: Example temporal position (column 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second column listed the number of class meetings that had occurred since the formal definition of a group had been given that the example at hand demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code temporal position so example neighborhood can be situated in time. Treat a written homework assignment as occurring on the day it was assigned. This helps describe approximate position in the example neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example qualities / properties (column 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third column described the qualities of the example or non-example. For examples, list additional qualities known to students by midpoint of course (e.g., commutative, finite, cyclic). For non-examples, describe missing properties and additional properties present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to describe the range of permissible variation included in the enacted example space (e.g., commutativity, finiteness, cyclicity, operation type, set type). Example: mark a non-example as 'missing inverse for 0' or list 'non-commutative, infinite'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example enactment & function (column 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth column described the manner in which the example or non-example was made part of the classroom discourse as well as how the example was used; i.e., the example function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record how the example entered discourse (introduced, constructed, modified, used in discussion, assigned as homework, used to prove a claim, etc.) and how students were involved (worked on it in-class, assigned for submission). This column also informs inferences about student engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish suggested vs required problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between those problems that were suggested and those that were required when coding practice/homework examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because engagement outside class cannot be directly observed, mark problems as 'required/submitted' (high likelihood of student engagement) versus 'suggested' (variable engagement). Use this distinction when inferring student interaction with example space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable student engagement indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark whether students were observed to actively engage with the examples during class meetings (direct observation) versus not; make few claims about engagement outside class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only infer engagement from in-class observation (e.g., all students worked on example during class, class discussion, in-class construction). Outside-class engagement should be treated as uncertain unless required-submission evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe first example and early sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to the first example and what other examples are presented soon after; describe how examples vary from one to the next and whether they vary along more than one dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratively summarize the early sequence because early examples heavily shape students' initial example neighborhood and possible misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total variation in example space
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a description of the total variation in the qualities of the examples and non-examples that the students experienced across the analyzed period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize whether students saw a range across dimensions (sizes, commutativity, finiteness, standard vs non-standard operations, set types) and whether coverage is broad or constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation sequencing principle (Dienes recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Dienes' recommendation about minimizing the amount of variation from one example to the next (varying along one dimension at a time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing sequencing, note whether the instructor varied examples by one dimension at a time (recommended) or introduced multi-dimensional variation at once (not recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and sufficiency of non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Record number and nature of non-examples presented; describe properties missing and whether non-examples were later modified into examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether non-examples sufficiently illustrate limits of the concept. Note if non-examples are rare or quickly transformed into examples, which can limit students' understanding of boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity across algebraic dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate example diversity across algebra-relevant dimensions (commutativity vs non-commutativity, finite vs infinite, cyclic vs non-cyclic, range of sizes, standard vs non-standard operations, familiar vs novel sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly enumerate coverage (e.g., 'commutative groups of all sizes', 'first non-commutative group introduced on day 7') and identify gaps that could cause misconceptions (e.g., believing all groups are commutative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example construction methods (students' access to tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the methods for constructing examples that students are exposed to (e.g., remove problematic elements from a set; define a non-standard operation on a set so it becomes a group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record exemplar constructions shown by instructor and assess whether students had meaningful opportunity to learn how those methods were created (i.e., could they reproduce the method to generate novel examples?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function taxonomy of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify how examples are being used: (1) to illustrate definitions, (2) to instantiate statements of propositions after introduction, (3) to motivate the need for and introduce definitions, (4) to motivate claims prior to formal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code each example occurrence by function. Note whether examples are used to motivate versus to generalize/create theory; e.g., the paper prefers 'motivate' when no generalization from examples was observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor use frequency and exemplar dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Track frequency of invocation for particular examples (e.g., (Z,+) used most frequently) and consider whether a heavily-invoked exemplar may occupy a preeminent status in students' concept image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess risk that a frequent exemplar (especially if it has extra properties) may skew students' reconstruction of the formal definition (e.g., thinking all groups are cyclic or commutative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of examples to homework/exam tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Record how many practice/homework/exam problems required students to work with specific examples or decide whether a structure is a group/subgroup, and whether these assignments were likely to elicit engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note required-submission tasks (high engagement) and the mix of example vs non-example problems in assignments (e.g., eight problems: five non-examples, three examples). Use this to infer likely student exposure and practice with variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and concentration of example-rich periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify class periods that drew on more examples per day than others and consider these best illustrations of teaching with examples (e.g., days immediately following introduction of formal definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporal clustering to prioritize analysis—periods with high example density are most informative about enacted example space and sequencing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples to illustrate proofs/theorems vs. motivate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether examples are used to exemplify propositions/theorems after formal statements or used pre-formally to motivate claims (and whether instructor generalizes from examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code instances where examples were used in proving or illustrating the proof versus those used only as motivation. Note the absence of generalization when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive claims about student learning from example exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw inferences about students' ability to learn and likelihood of learning based on the example space and student engagement evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the documented example neighborhood, construction methods exposure, functions of examples, and engagement indicators to hypothesize possible student misconceptions and likely learning outcomes; treat these as hypotheses needing empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological documentation for enacted-curriculum study
rubrics_metrics.description: Document data collection procedures for studying enacted curriculum: video-record consecutive class meetings, place camera to capture instructor and board, collect all handouts (homework/exams), track assigned practice problems, digitize video, and code incidents (showed/constructed/analyzed examples) using qualitative software (e.g., Transana).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rigorous, replicable procedures for capturing enacted examples. Code example incidents consistently and tie them to handouts/homework items and temporal position.
